title: UK and US crochet terminology
subtitle: Two parallel naming systems for the same stitches — translate before you start, not mid-row
excerpt: UK and US crochet conventions name the same stitches differently. UK double crochet is US single crochet. UK treble is US double crochet. The translation table is short, but the consequence of mixing them is a piece twice or half the intended size.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book, documents the UK/US naming convention conflict in detail. Both conventions trace to nineteenth-century crochet publishing — Therese de Dillmont's Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886) uses the UK convention; American manuals of the same period use the US set.

glossaryTerms.definition: Working part of a pattern in UK convention and part in US convention. The result: stitches that should be the same height are different by a full step. The canonical crochet bug.

content.text: UK and US crochet conventions name the same stitches differently. The moves are identical; the names are not. UK double crochet equals US single crochet. UK treble equals US double crochet. The translation table is short, but the consequence of mixing the two mid-pattern is a piece twice or half the intended size.

Homemade publishes in UK convention by default — UK names and abbreviations across all body prose. The reader-side terminology toggle in the page header flips abbreviations to US for readers who prefer the US set. Pick a convention before you start a pattern from elsewhere; the
convention mismatch
bug is the most-common crochet error.
The translation table
UK chain (ch) = US chain (ch). The same name.
UK slip stitch (sl st) = US slip stitch (sl st). The same name.
UK double crochet (dc) = US single crochet (sc). The first famous shift.
UK half treble (htr) = US half double crochet (hdc).
UK treble (tr) = US double crochet (dc). The second famous shift — US "dc" means something different from UK "dc".
UK double treble (dtr) = US treble (tr). Another full-step shift.
UK triple treble (trtr) = US double treble (dtr).
How to tell which convention a pattern uses
The pattern usually says so at the top — "written in UK terminology" or "US terms". If the pattern doesn't say, the publisher gives it away:
British publications (Pauline Turner, Stylecraft pattern leaflets, most UK magazines, anything from the British Library archive) write UK convention by default.
American publications (Annie's, Leisure Arts, most US magazines, US Ravelry self-published patterns) write US convention by default.
International publications (Japanese chart-driven books) usually use UK convention in the written instructions and the international symbol set in the charts.
If a pattern uses the abbreviation "sc" anywhere, it's US convention. If it uses the abbreviation "htr" anywhere, it's UK convention. The single most reliable signal.
Translating a US pattern to UK convention

Read the whole pattern through once first. Replace every abbreviation according to the translation table — "sc" becomes "dc", "dc" becomes "tr", "hdc" becomes "htr". Don't translate stitch by stitch as you work; that's where mistakes creep in. Translate the whole pattern on paper or in a notes app first, then work from the translated copy.

Watch for these gotchas: the turning chain count differs slightly between conventions for some stitches. UK treble takes a 3-chain turning chain that counts; US double crochet (the same stitch) sometimes takes a 2-chain turning chain that does not count, depending on the pattern's house style. Read the pattern's turning chain note carefully.
Worked example — translation in action
US pattern: "Row 2: ch 1 (does not count), sc in each st across (20 sts)."
UK translation: "Row 2: ch 1 (does not count), dc in each st across (20 sts)."
Same move, same height, same fabric. Only the abbreviation changed.
US pattern: "Round 1: in magic ring, ch 3 (counts as dc), 11 dc into ring. Sl st to top of beg ch-3. (12 dc.)"
UK translation: "Round 1: in magic ring, ch 3 (counts as tr), 11 tr into ring. Sl st to top of beg ch-3. (12 tr.)"
The US "dc" here is the UK "tr" — both name the same stitch (the workhorse pattern stitch of the granny square).
What to try next

Once the translation table feels familiar, every published crochet pattern in the world is readable in either convention. The next surface is hook size conversion — UK hooks use metric (4 mm), US hooks use letter-and-number combinations (G/6), Japanese hooks use Japanese-specific sizing. The CrochetHook reference table on every pattern page surfaces all three.
